notice: Blind grading of the storyline briefs, 21 Oct 2026. The versions are the published final stories of the runs named below; the judges saw them labelled A, B and C only, in the shuffled order the key records, and were asked to judge the writing, not the facts. Model output about model output: it decided a brief, not a fact.
rubric: hook, voice, specificity, cliche: 1-5 (5 best); overall: 1-10

claude-opus-5-5.summary: With the same facts and quotes on offer, placement decided most games: the winners put a narrative angle in the headline (White starting where Fiji lost a final, Scotland's route past England, Wales looking up at a side they beat) and let one dry line carry it, and the same Matfield or Faletau material read as wit in one version and filler in another. Ranking arithmetic appeared in every version and was the weakest writing everywhere; it survived only when compressed into one framed sentence ('the loser has further to fall') and failed as multi-outcome beats, back-to-back table lines or rating decimals, often straight after a first beat that restated the headline. The recurring tics were wire and press-release phrasing ('sharpening combinations', 'on Italian soil', 'the Brave Blossoms', 'pressing his case', 'Fifty-two weeks after'), and the six-beat versions that covered everything said least.

A.note: Press-release register ('sharpening combinations', 'billing as the Anniversary Test'), a Name: explainer headline and a closing beat of pure ranking arithmetic; the two-time-champions line is the one well-placed detail.

B.note: Headline carries the angle in seven words; the 31 applicants and the 'play like Fiji' quote are chosen rather than dumped, and the rankings beat is squeezed into 'the loser has further to fall'.

C.note: 'Fiji's response was to hire Jake White' and 'then the final' have the right dryness, but the headline only describes and 'a Japan defeat does the same to Japan' is a clumsy beat.

A.note: 'Close, mostly. Not wins.' is the knowledgeable friend at last, and the headline puts the stake in seven words; the 'table is tight' beat is filler.

B.note: Orderly, with a raised eyebrow in 'Farrell's stated target is the title', but the form beat is a string of scores and the headline has less snap for the same stake.

C.note: Six beats and no spine: 'flourishing display', 'pressing his case' and the Connacht aside are filler, and '6 of 8' / '1 of 6' are arithmetic standing in for a point.

A.note: 'Can only lose a place' is a real angle held through the first beat, 'the table says why that is unlikely' is the right dry turn, and the du Preez hamstring is genuine team news; the minus 94 / plus 81 line is table filler.

B.note: Headline crams two stakes in with 'topple', beat two is wire copy ('international rugby returns to...') and beat one repeats the headline; the unused 'last win 23-18 over England in March' is the best detail.

C.note: Tidy, with 'still on zero' and 'neither gets a rest' in the right register, but no single angle and a limp Matfield quote.

A.note: Wire-service preview: 'hit Murrayfield', 'arrive hot', 'locked on', 'injury list keeps mounting', and a closing beat that quotes rating points to two decimals.

B.note: Generic headline ('another shot') over clean beats: the stakes plus Australia arriving the week after in two sentences, and a McKenzie/Marshall beat with a quote that earns its place ('niggly at the breakdown').

C.note: Headline and opening beat set an angle (the route above England) and hold it; the Kerr beat is garnish, and 'doesn't get much bigger than that' is a cliche in quotation marks.

A.note: Competent and compact: the 12th-to-9th climb is well framed and Faletau is a good detail, but the headline states the fact without a sting and the angle isn't pushed.

B.note: Label headline ('a rankings swap in Cardiff'); two beats are arithmetic and a table line, and the squad beat lists names to no purpose ('Faletau misses out' and that is all).

C.note: Covers everything and commits to nothing: six beats, 'a new man in charge', records as '6 of 8', a table line; the one fresh thread (Vakatawa) is dropped after a single beat.

A.note: 'Vault' in the headline is hype and 'the ranking swap is live' is jargon; the last beat says Matfield 'has set out what they need' without saying what, then repeats beat one.

claude-sonnet-5-5.summary: The stronger versions chose one angle (the stake, the reversal, the pundit doubting the prize), put it in the headline and first beat, and squeezed the rankings arithmetic into one beat; the weaker ones gave every beat equal weight and let table lines, records like '6 of 8', crowd sizes and even rating decimals crowd out the story. Dry voice was rare and usually confined to a single line ('Close, mostly. Not wins.', 'on paper at least'), and the common failure was wire-service register ('arrive hot', 'pressing his case', 'rugby returns to'), which also supplied most of the clichés. Headlines varied most: the best state the angle with a turn, the worst are 'Name: explainer' labels or 'X hit Y' preview-speak.
